Every span includes the same correlation_id. This allows the tracing backend to link spans from different services (gateway, retrieval, agent, tool servers) into one distributed trace.
The model ID and version are captured from the API response metadata and logged with the span. Critical for correlating regressions with model updates.
The exact model version (date-stamped) is logged. If accuracy drops on June 11, logs can isolate requests served by the new version vs. the prior version.
Cache read/write tokens are logged as metadata. Helps track caching effectiveness and diagnose cost anomalies.
In production, each span is sent to Datadog / Honeycomb / Jaeger. Query by correlation_id to reconstruct the end-to-end trace.

e04_cost_model.out: Baseline: $66k/year (all Sonnet, no caching). Optimized: $20.6k/year (prompt caching + tiered routing to Haiku). Savings: $45.4k (68.7%).
a: Cache write is billed at the same price as input tokens ($3/M for Sonnet). Cache read is ~10% of input ($0.30/M for Sonnet).
The 3k-token system prompt is cached. Assume 10 sessions per cache TTL (~5 min). Each session pays 1/10 of the write cost (amortized).
9 out of 10 sessions read the cached system prompt at $0.30/M (vs. $3/M for fresh input). 90% savings on those 3k tokens.
60% of routine queries → Haiku (fast, cheap). 40% of complex queries → Sonnet (capable). Weighted average cost drops significantly.
Haiku input: $0.25/M (12× cheaper than Sonnet $3/M). Output: $1.25/M (12× cheaper than Sonnet $15/M). Most sessions fit Haiku's quality bar.
Combining prompt caching (targets the 45% static preamble cost) + tiered routing (sends 60% to Haiku) yields 68.7% overall savings without quality loss.

e01_rbac_rag: Only billing-related documents were retrieved. Clinical diagnosis notes (category="diagnosis") were filtered out at the retrieval layer because the user (billing_clerk_22) has permissions=["billing", "demographics"].
Citations reference the source document ID. The response is grounded in retrieved content.
First request: cache miss (0 read), cache write (1847 tokens = system prompt + context). Subsequent requests within ~5 min would show 1847 read, 0 write (90% cost savings).
e02_hipaa_config: Claude Enterprise is required for HIPAA BAA eligibility.
Business Associate Agreement with Anthropic executed.
Zero Data Retention - PHI is processed transiently but not retained by Anthropic.
7 years of audit logs (HIPAA requirement) showing who accessed which patient's PHI.
Prompt-level out-of-scope definitions + output classifier + tool hooks (defense in depth).
e03_observability: Same UUID across all three spans (gateway, retrieval, model). Querying by this ID reconstructs the full distributed trace.
Exact model version (claude-sonnet-4-20250610) captured on the model span. Critical for isolating regressions caused by model updates.
Prompt caching in effect: 3200 tokens read from cache (cheaper, faster prefill). Cache write would appear on the first request.
Per-request cost estimate: (4820 input - 3200 cached) × $3/M + 3200 × $0.30/M + 340 output × $15/M = ~$0.047.
e04_cost_model: All Sonnet, no caching. 8k avg input × $3/M + 600 output × $15/M = $0.033/session × 2M = $66k/year.
Prompt caching (3k-token system prompt cached) + tiered routing (60% Haiku, 40% Sonnet). Blended cost: $0.0103/session.
Caching cuts the 45% static-preamble cost by ~90%. Tiered routing sends 60% of traffic to Haiku (12× cheaper than Sonnet). Combined: 68.7% savings.

questions.q: An enterprise invoice-processing platform currently runs seven specialized agents that account for approximately 40 percent of engineering maintenance hours. Leadership has asked you to evaluate moving to managed agent infrastructure to reduce engineering overhead. The security officer requires that all customer financial data remain within an approved network boundary. Which factor should most heavily influence your recommendation?
o: whether managed agents support the current bus topology used by the platform team
whether managed agent data handling satisfies the network boundary required by security
whether managed agents reduce per-invoice token costs across the existing processing volume
whether the current seven agents map cleanly to the patterns supported by managed agents
questions.w: Hard security, compliance, and network-boundary / data-residency requirements act as non-negotiable gating constraints in enterprise architecture. Before evaluating cost savings (C), topology preferences (A), or migration convenience (D), the architect must verify whether the managed agent service satisfies the required security boundary.
questions.x: Options A, C, D address secondary concerns (topology, cost, migration ease) but ignore the mandatory security constraint. In enterprise architecture, SLA/compliance/security gates must be satisfied first.

questions.q: You are identifying the highest-impact optimization for a deployment whose requests carry a long, repeated system prompt and a large retrieved context per request. Which optimization most directly targets the dominant cost driver?
o: Move the long, repeated system prompt into a cacheable prefix and trim retrieved context to the spans relevant to each query.
Route simpler requests to a smaller model and reserve the larger model for cases that a lightweight classifier flags as complex.
Compress the system prompt by rewriting its instructions more concisely and removing examples that overlap with one another.
Batch requests so that several queries share a single call and the system prompt is transmitted once for the whole group.
questions.w: When input cost is dominated by a long static system prompt and large retrieved context per call, placing the repeated system prompt into a cacheable prefix (Prompt Caching) slashes repeat prefix token costs by up to 90%, while trimming retrieved passages to only the relevant spans directly reduces the variable per-request input token volume.
questions.x: B (tiered routing) helps but does not target the stated dominant drivers (long prompt + large context). C (compress prompt) may degrade quality. D (batching) does not fit most interactive workflows.

questions.q: You are selecting a protocol for a single low-latency lookup against an internal pricing service that already exposes a well-documented, stable HTTP API. Which integration mechanism is the most appropriate?
o: a direct API call to the existing endpoint with the appropriate scoped credentials
a long-lived stateful session protocol maintained between the assistant and the pricing service
an agent-to-agent handoff that introduces another Claude-based agent in front of the pricing service
a bespoke streaming protocol layered over an unrelated asynchronous message bus
questions.w: For a single, stateless, low-latency lookup against an existing HTTP API, a direct tool/API call using scoped credentials is the simplest, fastest, and most reliable mechanism. Introducing stateful sessions (B), extra agent hops (C), or custom streaming buses (D) adds unnecessary latency and complexity.
questions.x: B/C/D introduce unnecessary complexity and latency for a simple stateless lookup.

questions.q: You are distinguishing functional from non-functional requirements for a new Claude deployment. Which item is a non-functional requirement?
o: The system must classify inbound tickets into a defined set of categories and route each to the owning team.
The system must respond at p95 latency under 800 milliseconds at the expected request volume.
The system must produce a draft response that a human reviewer can edit before sending.
The system must extract a defined set of specific fields from invoice attachments and populate a downstream data record.
questions.w: Non-functional requirements specify system quality attributes, operational constraints, and performance SLAs—such as p95 response latency under 800ms at target load (B). Options A, C, and D describe functional behaviors and outputs.
questions.x: A, C, D are functional (what the system does). B is non-functional (how well it performs).

questions.q: A platform team at an organization needs to reduce both token cost and response latency for a high-volume assistant without degrading output quality on the core use case. Which two optimizations directly target both cost and latency simultaneously? (Select two.)
o: Expand the system prompt to include additional few-shot examples for edge cases.
Add a retrieval step that fetches the full source corpus into the context window before generation.
Enable prompt caching on the static system-prompt prefix to reduce billable input tokens on repeated calls.
Increase max_tokens to reduce the frequency of truncated responses requiring follow-up calls.
Route straightforward query types to a smaller, faster Claude model and reserve the full model for complex cases.
questions.w: Enabling prompt caching on the static prefix (C) reduces both input token cost and time-to-first-token (TTFT) latency. Tiered model routing (E) sends routine queries to a smaller, faster, lower-cost model (such as Haiku) while reserving the larger model for complex queries, simultaneously reducing average cost and latency without sacrificing quality.
questions.x: A/B/D either increase cost/latency or do not target both simultaneously.

questions.q: You are preparing a HIPAA-eligible deployment that processes Protected Health Information (PHI). Which configuration supports HIPAA compliance using Anthropic's offered controls?
o: Claude Enterprise with a signed Business Associate Agreement, Zero Data Retention enabled, and audit logging configured for compliance tracking
Claude Pro with no signed Business Associate Agreement, since a paid consumer subscription is sufficient to meet HIPAA requirements out of the box
an ad-hoc personal Claude account used by individual clinicians for PHI-related tasks, with no Business Associate Agreement, no Zero Data Retention, and no audit logging configured
Claude Team with a signed Business Associate Agreement but Zero Data Retention left disabled and audit logging not yet configured on the deployment
questions.w: Handling Protected Health Information (PHI) under HIPAA requires an enterprise-grade agreement with a signed Business Associate Agreement (BAA), Zero Data Retention (ZDR) enabled so PHI is not persisted, and comprehensive audit logging.
questions.x: B (Pro) lacks BAA. C (ad-hoc account) is non-compliant. D (Team with BAA but ZDR disabled) violates retention rules.

questions.q: You are selecting a Claude model for a new production workload. Which two steps must be completed BEFORE running a benchmark across candidate models? (Select two.)
o: Sign off the production rollout plan with the platform and security teams.
Choose a candidate model based on the requirements profile.
Retest the model choice when a new model version becomes available.
Define the quality bar, latency tolerance, and expected volume for the workload.
Select the lightest model that consistently meets the quality bar across the sample.
questions.w: Following the standard 5-step model alignment sequence: first define the quality bar, latency tolerance, and expected volume for the workload (D), and second choose candidate models based on that requirements profile (B). Running the benchmark, selecting the lightest model that meets the bar (E), signing off rollout (A), and retesting when new models launch (C) all happen during or after benchmarking.
questions.x: A/C/E happen after benchmarking, not before.

questions.q: A Claude-assisted knowledge workflow retrieves passages from external documents and summarizes them for analysts. You need to reduce ungrounded claims in the generated output. Which control most directly reduces ungrounded claims in the output?
o: tightening the eval configuration on fewer, generic test cases
treating retrieved passages as untrusted input and screening them for injection
constraining responses to source-supported content combined with required citations
scoring each new model version against a stable adversarial evaluation set before promotion
questions.w: To directly prevent ungrounded claims (hallucinations) in a retrieval-augmented generation workflow, you must constrain the model to rely strictly on source-supported content and require verifiable citations back to the retrieved passages (C). Screening retrieved passages (B) defends against indirect prompt injection rather than hallucination.
questions.x: A (fewer test cases) weakens eval. B prevents injection, not hallucination. D detects problems after the fact, does not prevent.

questions.q: A healthcare organization is evaluating two Claude-based architectures for clinical documentation. Architecture X achieves higher clinical quality scores, costs $0.18 per session, and averages 4.2 seconds per response. Architecture Y scores slightly lower on quality metrics, but costs $0.09 per session and averages 2.1 seconds per response. The clinical SLA requires responses under 3 seconds, and volume is projected at 2 million sessions annually. Which evaluation approach correctly applies business value pillar analysis to this decision?
o: Select Architecture X because the higher quality scores justify the cost premium, and address the latency gap through infrastructure optimization after deployment.
Select Architecture Y based solely on the 50% cost reduction, since solution cost is the primary consideration in budget-constrained environments.
Recommend a hybrid approach using Architecture X for complex cases and Architecture Y for routine cases, since this preserves quality where it matters most.

Eliminate Architecture X on SLA grounds, then evaluate Architecture Y against the efficiency and solution cost pillars by calculating annual cost difference and assessing whether the quality delta materially impacts clinical workflow productivity.
questions.w: Architecture X averages 4.2 seconds, violating the mandatory <3-second clinical SLA, so it must be eliminated on technical SLA grounds first. Architecture Y (2.1s) meets the SLA and must then be evaluated across the solution-cost pillar ($180,000/yr vs. $360,000/yr at 2M sessions) and the efficiency pillar (whether the slight quality delta affects clinician review time).
questions.x: A keeps a design that violates the SLA. B/C do not apply SLA elimination first.

questions.q: A Claude-based assistant begins exhibiting a regression in citation grounding after a recent model and system-prompt update. Which two diagnostic actions most directly isolate the root cause? (Select two.)
o: Inspect system-prompt grounding instructions to determine whether citation constraints were weakened.
Isolate whether the failure reproduces on the previous model version to separate model change from prompt change.
Increase the context window size to allow more retrieved chunks per query.
Reduce the temperature setting to lower response variance across all query types.
Switch the retrieval index to a denser embedding model to improve chunk relevance scores.
questions.w: When a regression follows a simultaneous prompt and model update, inspecting the system-prompt grounding instructions (A) and testing whether the issue reproduces on the prior model version while holding the prompt constant (B) directly isolate which change caused the failure.
questions.x: C/D/E address different problems (context size, variance, retrieval quality) and do not isolate the root cause of a regression after a prompt+model update.

questions.q: You are defining where human review must sit in an agentic workflow. Which placement reflects sound human-in-the-loop design?
o: Place a human reviewer between each incoming request and the model so inputs are checked before generation.
Place a human reviewer between the model's output and any high-impact, irreversible action.
Place a human reviewer between the model's output and any action a confidence score marks as uncertain.
Place a human reviewer between the model's output and every action, regardless of impact or reversibility.
questions.w: Sound human-in-the-loop (HITL) architecture places human approval gates specifically between model outputs/tool proposals and high-impact, irreversible actions (such as sending external payouts, deleting records, or executing legal commitments). Reviewing every low-risk read-only step (D) destroys automation value, and relying solely on uncalibrated model confidence scores (C) can miss confident errors.
questions.x: A reviews inputs (wrong focus). C relies on uncalibrated confidence. D destroys automation value.

questions.q: You are integrating AI-assisted documentation generation into a software engineering team's repository workflow so documentation stays accurate and reviewed. Which integration approach best fits this requirement?
o: Configure subagents that read the relevant code files and generate documentation, publishing directly to the shared documentation site.
Configure subagents that read a small sample of the repository's files and generate documentation from that sample, then route it through review.
Configure subagents that read the relevant code files and draft documentation, then have a single reviewer spot-check one section before publication.
Configure subagents that read the relevant code files via filesystem and code-search tools, generate the documentation draft, and route the changes through the team's normal review workflow.
questions.w: Giving subagents full read-only access to the relevant code files via filesystem and code-search tools ensures the drafted documentation is grounded in the real implementation, while routing the generated changes through the engineering team's standard pull-request review workflow guarantees human verification before publication.
questions.x: A bypasses review. B uses incomplete input. C spot-checks (insufficient). D ensures grounding + review.

questions.q: A managed agent deployed for claims triage has grown to 34 tools, and tool-selection accuracy has declined from 91 percent to 75 percent. A colleague proposes placing a router agent in front of the current agent. Which two findings should you present to justify capability decomposition and tool cleanup before adding a router? (Select two.)
o: Several tools have not been invoked across the most recent 60 days of traffic.
The proposed router introduces an additional model call on every incoming request.
The router pattern is well-documented across publicly available agent literature.
The 34 tools serve four distinct claim workflow domains within the triage scope.
Tool descriptions overlap across multiple claim categories within the agent's tool set.
questions.w: The drop in tool-selection accuracy from 91% to 75% is caused by packing 34 tools across four distinct domains (D) with overlapping tool descriptions (E) into a single agent (along with unused tools, A), while adding a router agent adds extra latency/cost on every request (B). Decomposing by domain and disambiguating overlapping tool descriptions directly fixes the root cause.
questions.x: A (unused tools) is cleanup, but not the core justification. B (extra call) is a downside of the router. C (well-documented) is irrelevant.

questions.q: You are auditing a procurement-assistant agent whose scoped task is to look up catalog items, check procurement policy, and prepare purchase-request drafts for human approval. The agent currently has these five tools configured: (1) read-only catalog lookup, (2) inbox-send tool that emails vendors directly, (3) draft-write tool that creates requests in the review queue, (4) production-database admin tool unrelated to procurement, (5) read-only policy-document tool. After a least-privilege audit, which tools should remain?
o: Keep tools 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (all tools needed)
Keep tools 1, 3, 5 (catalog lookup, draft-write, policy lookup); remove tools 2, 4
Keep tools 1, 2, 5; remove tools 3, 4
Keep only tool 1 (catalog lookup); remove all others
questions.w: Only tools required for the agent's scoped read/draft duties (catalog lookup, policy lookup, and draft-queue creation) remain; tools that bypass human approval (direct vendor email) or grant unrelated admin privileges are removed.
questions.x: Tool 2 bypasses approval (sends emails directly to vendors without human review). Tool 4 is unrelated to procurement (admin access not needed). Tools 1, 3, 5 are needed for the agent's scope.

questions.q: You are reviewing observability instrumentation in a production multi-turn agent deployment. Which two findings constitute valid observability gaps in the architecture? (Select two.)
o: Request-scoped correlation identifiers are omitted across downstream tool and subagent calls.
Latency and token usage on every span are emitted to the telemetry pipeline.
Trace spans for each agent step are exported to the shared distributed-tracing backend.
Model identity and version on each turn are not recorded with the turn artifacts.
Tool-call payloads and outcomes are recorded with redaction applied to known sensitive fields.
questions.w: Omitting request-scoped correlation IDs across tool/subagent boundaries (A) prevents reconstructing end-to-end distributed traces, and failing to log the model identity and version per turn (D) makes it impossible to correlate regressions with model updates. Options B, C, and E represent healthy observability practices.
questions.x: B/C/E are healthy practices (emitting metrics, exporting spans, logging with redaction). A/D are gaps.

questions.q: You are reviewing a peer's draft Architecture Decision Record (ADR). The ADR states the decision clearly, but omits the alternatives considered and the trade-offs accepted. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Publish the ADR as written and open a follow-up task to add alternatives later.
Approve the ADR as written since the decision is documented, treating the missing sections as optional.
Ask the author to add the alternatives considered and the trade-offs accepted before publishing the ADR.
Ask the author to link the design-discussion thread in place of a written alternatives section.
questions.w: An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) must capture not only what was decided, but also the rejected alternatives and accepted trade-offs so future teams understand the rationale and constraints behind the choice.
questions.x: A/B/D leave the ADR incomplete. C ensures the ADR preserves context for future teams.

questions.q: You are a solution architect reviewing an agent that loads 60 tool definitions into the context window on every request, consuming substantial input tokens and increasing latency. Which design pattern best addresses this issue without sacrificing capability?
o: Increase the maximum context length so all 60 tool definitions fit comfortably.
Group the 60 tools into five fixed categories and load one category per request based on a static keyword rule.
Use a separate model call to condense all 60 tool definitions into a compact index that is prepended to every prompt.
Apply progressive tool discovery so a curated initial subset is exposed and additional tools are loaded on demand.
questions.w: Progressive / on-demand tool discovery (such as Tool Search / `expand_tools`) exposes only a minimal core set initially and dynamically loads additional tool definitions when the conversation requires them, cutting baseline token overhead while retaining access to all 60 tools.
questions.x: A increases cost/latency without fixing selection. B is brittle (static keyword rules miss nuance). C loses the actual definitions. D (progressive discovery) solves it.

questions.q: A finance operations team is evaluating how much decision authority to delegate to an AI-assisted workflow. Which principle reflects sound Delegation competency?
o: Delegation scope should be set primarily by maximizing efficiency gains across the workflow.
Delegation scope should include human review on high-consequence, irreversible decisions the workflow produces.
Delegation should be avoided in most cases wherever financial data appears anywhere in the workflow.
Delegation should generally exclude human review on decisions the workflow produces, independent of consequence.
questions.w: Under the AI Fluency Framework's Delegation competency, delegation scope is governed by task reversibility and error consequence: high-impact or irreversible decisions require human review and accountability.
questions.x: A ignores consequence. C is too broad. D removes accountability. B correctly gates high-consequence decisions with human review.

questions.q: Users report that a deployed summarization assistant has occasionally fabricated citations in its summaries. Which two immediate diagnostic and containment actions should you take? (Select two.)
o: Sample recent summaries to estimate the fabrication frequency across the user population.
Review whether citation grounding controls exist anywhere in the current generation pipeline.
Communicate to users that the assistant does not fabricate output as a matter of design.
Lower the model's sampling temperature across the pipeline in response to the incident.
Disable the assistant immediately for all current users without any prior diagnostic analysis.
questions.w: When ungrounded citations are reported in production, you should immediately quantify the scope/frequency of the issue by sampling recent outputs (A) and audit the generation pipeline to check whether citation grounding/verification controls are present and functioning (B).
questions.x: C (deny fabrication) is false. D (lower temperature) is a guess. E (disable without diagnosis) is premature. A+B are immediate diagnostic actions.

questions.q: You are conducting a security review of an agent architecture specification. Which two findings constitute valid security gaps in the specification? (Select two.)
o: Tool inputs and outputs are encrypted in transit using transport layer security (TLS).
Service credentials are placed in the prompt context where they can leak into logs and traces.
Per-user OAuth tokens are exchanged with scope-restricted permissions and refreshed for the active session.
Tool calls execute server-side under a least-privilege service principal scoped to the requested action.
Role-based access control (RBAC) is enforced only at the response-rendering layer after the model has generated its output.
questions.w: Placing service credentials inside the prompt context (B) exposes secrets to prompt injection and log leakage. Enforcing RBAC only at the UI/response-rendering layer after the model has already ingested restricted documents (E) allows unauthorized data into the model context where it can be inferred or leaked. Options A, C, and D are sound security controls.
questions.x: A/C/D are sound controls (TLS, scoped OAuth, least-privilege principals). B/E are gaps.

questions.q: A Claude architect is leading the discovery phase for a new enterprise AI initiative. Which two activities are characteristic of structured discovery and requirements gathering? (Select two.)
o: facilitating stakeholder workshops to surface latency, accuracy, and compliance constraints
deferring constraint documentation until the integration design phase to avoid premature scope limits
generating an initial prototype and iterating based on user reactions alone without formal criteria
documenting explicit success criteria and failure thresholds that will gate production deployment
selecting the Claude model tier based on the architect's prior project experience before stakeholder input is gathered
questions.w: Structured architectural discovery surfaces business, latency, accuracy, and compliance constraints upfront with stakeholders (A) and establishes measurable success criteria and failure thresholds to gate production rollout (D).
questions.x: B/C/E skip or defer discovery (constraints, criteria, model selection should follow discovery, not precede it).

questions.q: You are assembling the technical handoff documentation package for a production Claude deployment. Which documentation set belongs in the technical handoff package?
o: architecture overview, ADRs, component-level diagrams, runbooks, and known limitations
the original design proposal, its review comments, and raw meeting notes from design sessions
a project retrospective document, a lessons-learned summary, and a list of contributors
user-facing release notes, a marketing one-pager describing the deployment, and a customer FAQ
questions.w: An engineering and operations handoff package requires the living architectural artifacts needed to operate, troubleshoot, and evolve the system: the architecture overview, Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), component diagrams, operational runbooks, and documented system limitations.
questions.x: B (raw notes) is not actionable. C (retrospective) is post-project, not operational. D is user-facing, not engineering handoff.

questions.q: You are reviewing a peer's Claude Code permission rules for a shared repository and notice unrestricted Bash access is enabled across all developer workflows. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Replace unrestricted Bash with narrowly scoped tool patterns that allow required commands and add explicit deny rules for sensitive operations.
Approve the rules as written, treating Bash scoping as a matter for each project team to revisit later.
Allow-list Bash to the specific commands the workflows require, relying on the allow-list's implicit default deny alone without explicit deny guardrails.
Replace unrestricted Bash access with narrowly scoped tool patterns, but apply the exact same static pattern globally to every project regardless of each project's actual workflow needs.
questions.w: Claude Code security best practices replace unrestricted `Bash(*)` access with narrowly scoped command patterns tailored to the workflow combined with explicit deny rules blocking destructive or sensitive operations.
questions.x: B approves the risk. C omits explicit deny rules. D applies one-size-fits-all (not tailored). A is correct.

questions.q: You are defining production monitoring metrics to verify that an enterprise deployment stays within its per-query cost budget and meets its interactive responsiveness SLA. Which two metrics belong in the monitoring specification? (Select two.)
o: per-query token cost measured against the defined cost ceiling
throughput measured as successful requests processed per minute
BLEU score computed against a human-annotated reference summary set
role-based access-control enforcement rate measured on a red-team dataset
response latency at the 95th percentile across a one-week sample window
questions.w: To directly monitor the per-query cost ceiling and interactive responsiveness SLA, the deployment must track per-query token cost against the cost ceiling (A) and p95 response latency (E).
questions.x: B (throughput) does not measure cost or latency. C (BLEU) is quality, not SLA. D (RBAC enforcement rate) is security, not cost/latency.

questions.q: You are compiling continuity practices across a multi-phase Claude implementation so each phase builds cleanly on prior phases. Which two practices belong on the list? (Select two.)
o: Maintain a stakeholder register and notify the listed parties at every phase gate.
Lock decisions made in early phases to prevent revisiting them as later phases begin.
Capture lessons learned at the end of each phase and surface them as inputs to the next phase.
Carry the evaluation framework and reference set forward across iterations rather than rebuilding from scratch.
Archive every phase deliverable in long-term storage to preserve a record of what was produced.
questions.w: Iterative architectural continuity requires feeding lessons learned from each phase into the next phase's design (C) and carrying the evaluation framework and benchmark reference dataset forward across iterations to measure progress and prevent regressions (D).
questions.x: A (notify stakeholders) is good but not continuity. B (lock decisions) prevents evolution. E (archive) is record-keeping, not continuity.

questions.q: A retrieval-augmented assistant is missing its p95 latency target because each request retrieves and injects top-25 lengthy passages, even though historic trace analysis shows the answer is almost always contained in the top-5 passages and a small set of recurring questions accounts for 40% of traffic. Which optimization most directly reduces end-to-end latency while preserving answer quality?
o: Switch the vector database to a brute-force flat index.
Precompute and cache retrieval embeddings only.
Cache the full corpus in memory ahead of each request.
Reduce retrieval depth to the top-k passages that historically cover the answer and cache responses/contexts for frequent queries.
questions.w: Trimming `top-k` retrieval depth to the passages that empirically contain the answer reduces the input token count sent to the model (the main driver of prefill/TTFT latency), and caching frequent queries avoids redundant retrieval and generation altogether.
questions.x: A/B/C do not reduce input token count (the TTFT driver). D directly cuts input tokens and caches frequent queries.

questions.q: You are setting up operational monitoring and alerting for a new Claude deployment. Which two steps must be completed BEFORE building the monitoring dashboards and alert rules? (Select two.)
o: Document the dashboards, alerts, and runbooks for the on-call rotation.
Tune the alert thresholds based on observed normal-state distributions to reduce false alarms.
Build the dashboards that surface metrics across slices at the cadence the team operates.
Define the metrics and the slices the deployment will monitor across normal and adversarial traffic.
Define the service-level objectives (SLOs) and the error budgets the deployment will be held to.
questions.w: Before you can build dashboards (C), tune alert thresholds (B), or document dashboard runbooks (A), you must first define what metrics and data slices need to be measured (D) and what Service-Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets constitute acceptable performance (E).
questions.x: A/B/C happen after defining metrics/SLOs. D+E must come first.

questions.q: A daily sales-analysis workload runs thousands of queries against a Claude model. Cost breakdown shows a large static policy preamble repeated on every call (45 percent of cost), retrieved historical sales chunks (35 percent, with the same popular chunks retrieved across many daily queries), and output generation (20 percent). Stakeholders require no loss in reasoning quality. Which two optimizations should you sequence first to reduce cost? (Select two.)
o: Truncate the policy preamble to remove clauses from the prompt.
Cache common retrieved sales chunks accessed across many of the daily queries.
Switch the workload to a smaller, faster Claude model tier across all queries.
Reduce the number of historical sales chunks retrieved across each query run.
Enable prompt caching on the static policy preamble across the recurring calls.
questions.w: Enabling prompt caching on the static policy preamble (E, targeting 45% of cost) and caching frequently reused retrieved sales chunks in a stable prefix order (B, targeting 35% of cost) directly reduce input token costs without removing policy rules, dropping needed sales data, or downgrading model reasoning quality.
questions.x: A removes needed rules. C may degrade quality. D removes needed data. B+E target the dominant drivers without quality loss.

questions.q: You are reviewing a system prompt where one section instructs the model to answer strictly from provided sources, and another section instructs the model to fill in gaps using general knowledge when sources are incomplete. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Keep both contradictory instructions in place and let the model balance them based on context.
Add a priority-ordering instruction that tells the model to evaluate all available rules and pick one on each request.
Keep both contradictory instructions in place and rely on the model to select which one to follow, accepting inconsistent behavior as a result.
Resolve the contradiction by removing or rewording the gap-filling instruction so the prompt consistently enforces source-supported content.
questions.w: Contradictory instructions inside a system prompt cause unpredictable drift between grounded answers and unverified hallucinations. Removing or refactoring the conflicting gap-filling instruction ensures consistent adherence to source grounding.
questions.x: A/B/C leave the contradiction in place, causing inconsistent behavior. D resolves it.

questions.q: A security audit of an enterprise agent identifies that all users share a single static API key for downstream tool calls, credentials are included in prompt text, and RBAC is not enforced during retrieval. Which two remediations directly fix the credential and access-control vulnerabilities? (Select two.)
o: Replace the shared API key with scoped per-user authentication tokens.
Move credentials out of the prompt context and resolve them server-side at tool execution time.
Enforce RBAC at the retrieval layer before content enters the model context.
Validate structured outputs against a schema before downstream actions are executed.

domains.title: 1. Business Value Pillars, SLA Gating & Discovery
points: Business Value Pillars (concepts: SLA elimination + value pillar analysis · Compliance assessment sequence): Distinguish between Efficiency (processing 3x more POs per analyst per day), Transformation (retiring manual data entry roles and redeploying staff to vendor relationships), Solution Cost (API integration costs vs per-transaction budget), and Performance SLA (11s latency vs 3s committed SLA).

SLA Elimination Gate (concepts: SLA elimination + value pillar analysis): When evaluating architectures where Architecture X averages 4.2s against a strict 3-second SLA, eliminate Architecture X on SLA grounds first, then evaluate Architecture Y against efficiency and solution cost.

Non-Functional Requirements (concepts: HIPAA compliance configuration): Latency targets like 'respond at p95 latency under 800 milliseconds at expected request volume' are non-functional requirements (unlike classification or field extraction).

Discovery & ADRs (concepts: ADR completeness · Discovery workshop activities · Technical handoff documentation · Discovery session facilitation): Facilitate stakeholder workshops to surface latency, accuracy, and compliance constraints and document explicit success/failure deployment gates. ADRs must include alternatives considered and trade-offs accepted before publishing.

domains.title: 2. RAG Strategies, RBAC Retrieval & Token Lifecycle
points: Retrieval Strategy Matrix (concepts: Retrieval strategy characteristics): Dense vector retrieval excels at paraphrased intent on unstructured text; Sparse term-matching recovers exact terms (IDs, rare tokens) more reliably than dense alone; Structured query retrieval fits filter-and-aggregate workloads on relational stores; Hybrid retrieval is NOT identical to dense-only.

RBAC at the Retrieval Layer (concepts: Security architecture review · SLA monitoring metrics · Model selection principles · Workflow vs. agentic pattern selection): Enforce authentication, authorization, and role-based access control (RBAC) at the retrieval layer before any role-restricted content reaches prompt construction or the model—never rely on post-filtering or system-prompt instructions.

Cost & Latency Optimization (concepts: Cost optimization targeting dominant drivers · Model selection process · Monitoring setup sequence · Prompt contradiction resolution · Release governance / scope discipline): Enable prompt caching on static system-prompt/policy preambles or legal filings reused across queries, trim retrieved context to relevant top-k spans, cache common retrieved chunks, and route straightforward queries to smaller/faster models (Haiku).

Request Lifecycle Classification (concepts: Testing strategy for safety & regression · Diligence / AI-generated code review): Input Preparation: Trim retrieved passages to relevant spans; summarize prior history when full history isn't needed. Prompt Construction: Move stable repeated content into a cacheable prefix; order prompt sections so cacheable content sits before per-request content. Output Handling: Validate structured output against schema; persist validated output for audit.

domains.title: 3. Agent Tooling, Progressive Discovery & Least Privilege
points: Progressive Tool Discovery / Tool Search (concepts: Progressive tool discovery · Workflow vs. agentic pattern selection): When an assistant has 60+ tool definitions or multiple MCP servers exhausting the context budget upfront, enable Tool Search / progressive tool discovery so a curated initial subset is exposed and tool definitions are loaded on demand.

Capability Decomposition Before Routing (concepts: Capability decomposition justification): If an agent with 34 tools has declining triage accuracy (91% -> 78%), justify capability decomposition by showing the 34 tools serve 4 distinct workflow domains and tool descriptions overlap across categories.

Least-Privilege Tool Audits (concepts: Least-privilege tool audit · Model tier selection by workload): Retain only Category 1 & 2 tools (mapped to defined tasks and regular hand-offs), or strictly Category 1 minimal set. In procurement audits: keep read-only catalog lookup, read-only policy lookup, and draft-write queue tools; remove direct vendor inbox-send and unrelated prod-DB admin tools.

Human-in-the-Loop Placement (concepts: HITL placement · Incident response / troubleshooting): Place a human reviewer between the model's output and any high-impact, irreversible action. For financial refunds, include human review on decisions produced by the workflow.

domains.title: 4. Security, HIPAA Compliance, Guardrails & Observability
points: HIPAA Deployment (concepts: Integration pattern selection): Requires Claude Enterprise with a signed Business Associate Agreement (BAA), Zero Data Retention (ZDR) enabled, and audit logging configured.

Secrets, OAuth & Bash Scoping (concepts: Security architecture review · Scoped Bash permissions · Layered guardrails design): Move service credentials out of prompt context into a server-side secret store. Replace shared API keys with per-user OAuth tokens carrying scope-restricted permissions and add actor attribution to tool-call logs. Replace unrestricted Bash with narrowly-scoped tool patterns and explicit deny rules.

Layered Guardrails (concepts: Fairness evaluation / Discernment · Trade-off prioritization): Combine explicit out-of-scope refusal categories in the system prompt with runtime output classifiers and structured schema validation.

Observability & Experimentation (concepts: Observability instrumentation · Security remediation · A/B experiment design · Resilient guardrail architecture): Propagate request-scoped correlation IDs across agent/tool calls and record model identity/version on every turn. Before running A/B experiments, define hypothesis + primary metric and determine minimum detectable effect size/sample size.

domains.title: 1. Distributed Multi-Agent Mesh, Resilience & Idempotency
points: Hierarchical Orchestration & Blast-Radius Isolation: Combine deterministic state machines for high-volume happy paths with bounded subagent swarms for exception handling. Isolate subagent context windows so sub-task tool outputs never pollute the parent orchestrator's token budget.

Idempotent Tool Dispatch & Checkpointing: When resuming checkpointed long-running agents after mid-flight crashes, attach deterministic idempotency_key headers to all mutating tool calls (e.g., payment/ERP writes) so replayed turns never duplicate side effects.

Circuit Breakers & Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ): Wrap external MCP servers and downstream APIs in circuit breakers. If a downstream dependency trips or schema validation fails after bounded retries, route the serialized checkpoint payload to a Dead-Letter Queue for asynchronous human or automated replay.

Cross-Region Quota & Rate-Limit Federation: Use token-bucket admission controllers ahead of model invocation queues to smooth bursty traffic and route non-interactive overflow to the Message Batches API.

domains.title: 2. Federated RAG, Multi-Tenant Isolation & Context Compaction
points: Zero-Trust Multi-Tenant Retrieval: Enforce cryptographic tenant and RBAC claims at the query planner level before hybrid (Dense + Sparse BM25 + Graph) retrieval executes. Prevent cross-tenant cache poisoning by scoping prompt-cache prefixes per tenant security boundary.

Hierarchical Context Compaction: For multi-session enterprise workflows, implement a tiered memory architecture: hot active turn state (verbatim), warm session summary (structured JSON state), and cold episodic audit store.

Dynamic Retrieval Depth & Citation Verification: Dynamically adjust top_k based on query complexity classifier scores and run an automated post-generation NLI (Natural Language Inference) citation verifier before streaming final commitments to external customers.

domains.title: 3. Enterprise MCP Gateways, Zero-Trust Security & Policy-as-Code
points: Centralized MCP Gateway Architecture: Place an enterprise MCP Gateway between Claude agents and internal microservices to enforce per-user OAuth token exchange (OBO flow), progressive Tool Search indexing, schema validation, and centralized actor audit logging.

PII/PHI Tokenization Proxy: Redact or tokenize regulated identifiers (SSN, PAN, PHI) into reversible vault tokens at intake before prompt construction, detokenizing only in authorized downstream sinks.

Defense-in-Depth Guardrails: Layer
  1. Input sanitization & data-tag isolation
  2. System-prompt out-of-scope refusal rules
  3. Deterministic PreToolUse policy-as-code hooks (OPA/Cedar)
  4. Asynchronous/synchronous output classifiers

domains.title: 4. Production FinOps, SLO Error Budgets & CI/CD Evaluation Gates
points: Multi-Dimensional Evaluation Pipelines: Gate every prompt, Skill, or model-version change in CI/CD against a stratified evaluation dataset covering representative traffic, edge cases, demographic/tenure slices, and adversarial prompt-injection payloads.

Shadow & Canary Model Rollouts: When migrating to a new pinned model snapshot, run shadow traffic and statistically powered A/B experiments (pre-calculating minimum detectable effect size and sample size) while monitoring slice-level error budgets.

Unit-Economics Attribution: Track cost-per-resolved-outcome (combining input/output tokens, cache read/write ratios, tool-call retries, and human-escalation rate) rather than raw per-request token cost alone.

matrix.trigger: Where should Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) be enforced in a RAG pipeline?
matrix.action: At the retrieval layer, before any role-restricted content reaches the prompt construction step or the model (concepts: Workflow vs. agentic pattern selection)

matrix.trigger: Security audit finds shared API keys, credentials in prompts, or missing user attribution in tool logs
matrix.action: Replace shared key with per-user scoped OAuth tokens, move credentials to server-side secret store, add actor attribution to logs (concepts: Security architecture review · Layered guardrails design)

matrix.trigger: Peer's Claude Code config grants unrestricted Bash access to all projects
matrix.action: Replace unrestricted Bash with narrowly-scoped tool patterns required by workflows and add explicit deny rules for sensitive ops (concepts: Scoped Bash permissions)

matrix.trigger: Architecture X has higher quality but 4.2s average latency vs a mandatory 3.0s SLA; Architecture Y is 2.1s and 50% cheaper
matrix.action: Eliminate Architecture X on SLA grounds first, then evaluate Architecture Y against efficiency and solution cost pillars (concepts: SLA elimination + value pillar analysis)

matrix.trigger: 60+ tool definitions or many MCP servers exhaust context budget and increase time-to-first-token
matrix.action: Apply progressive tool discovery / enable Tool Search so tool definitions are deferred and loaded on demand (concepts: Progressive tool discovery · Workflow vs. agentic pattern selection)

matrix.trigger: Legal document service runs 14 queries per filing, and security forbids storing filing contents outside the tenant
matrix.action: Cache the filing as the prompt prefix for reuse across the 14 queries per case (concepts: Release governance / scope discipline)

matrix.trigger: High-volume content moderation classifier under a tight per-message latency budget with well-defined labels
matrix.action: Select Haiku (lightweight, lowest latency, lowest cost for structured classification) (concepts: MCP vs. direct API integration)

matrix.trigger: Batch document processing with well-defined steps: extract, classify, summarize, persist
matrix.action: A workflow pattern, because steps are well-defined and predictable per-request token cost is preferred over flexibility (concepts: Model tier selection by workload)

matrix.trigger: Compliance regulatory procedure changes 4-6 times/year and is used across 3 separate workflows
matrix.action: Package the procedure as a Claude Skill owned by compliance + reference the same Skill from all 3 workflow integrations (concepts: Skill-based reuse)

matrix.trigger: Loan pre-qualification assistant has 94% match with human underwriters and equal approval rates across groups
matrix.action: Match with human underwriters does not establish freedom from underwriter bias + Approval rate parity does not assess error rate parity (concepts: AI ethics review)

matrix.trigger: Resuming a checkpointed agent that crashed mid-execution while calling a mutating ERP/payment tool
matrix.action: Pass a deterministic idempotency key derived from (task_id + step_index + tool_call_id) on every mutating tool dispatch

matrix.trigger: Multi-tenant SaaS RAG assistant uses Prompt Caching; security warns about cross-tenant data leakage
matrix.action: Partition cacheable prefixes by tenant_id and enforce tenant + RBAC filters at the retrieval layer before prompt construction

matrix.trigger: Enterprise has 200+ internal tools across 15 teams; needs unified OAuth scoping, audit logs, and low token overhead
matrix.action: Deploy a centralized MCP Gateway with On-Behalf-Of (OBO) per-user OAuth token exchange and progressive Tool Search

matrix.trigger: Upgrading a pinned Claude model version in a regulated financial/healthcare workflow
matrix.action: Run the candidate model against the stratified + adversarial evaluation dataset in CI/CD, verify parity across slices, then canary rollout

matrix.trigger: Subagent responsible for deep code/log analysis floods the orchestrator's context window with 40k tokens of raw logs
matrix.action: Isolate the subagent's context window and require it to return only a validated, schema-constrained synthesis to the orchestrator

matrix.trigger: Latency spikes during end-of-month traffic bursts threaten p95 SLA on a mixed interactive + reporting workload
matrix.action: Decouple bursty intake with an async queue, route interactive simple queries to Haiku, and offload non-interactive reports to Batch API

code.title: Enterprise MCP Gateway with OBO OAuth, Idempotency & PreToolUse Policy Hook
code.description: Synthesizes Developer Pro and Architect Foundation patterns into a production MCP dispatcher with per-user OAuth exchange, schema validation, deterministic policy checks, and idempotency keys.
code.code:
import hashlib
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class ExecutionContext:
    correlation_id: str
    tenant_id: str
    user_oauth_token: str
    model_version: str
    task_id: str
    step_index: int

class EnterpriseMCPGateway:
    def __init__(self, secret_store, policy_engine, audit_logger):
        self.secret_store = secret_store
        self.policy_engine = policy_engine
        self.audit_logger = audit_logger

    async def dispatch_tool(self, ctx: ExecutionContext, tool_use_block: dict) -> dict:
        tool_name = tool_use_block["name"]
        tool_input = tool_use_block["input"]
        tool_call_id = tool_use_block["id"]

        # 1. Validate arguments against registered JSON Schema before dispatch
        if not self.policy_engine.validate_schema(tool_name, tool_input):
            return {"is_error": True, "content": "SchemaValidationError: Invalid tool arguments"}

        # 2. Deterministic PreToolUse Policy-as-Code Gate (blocks destructive/unauthorized ops)
        decision = self.policy_engine.evaluate_pre_tool_hook(
            user_token=ctx.user_oauth_token,
            tenant_id=ctx.tenant_id,
            tool_name=tool_name,
            tool_input=tool_input
        )
        if not decision.allowed:
            if decision.requires_human_approval:
                return {"status": "PENDING_HITL_APPROVAL", "approval_Queue_id": decision.queue_id}
            return {"is_error": True, "content": f"PolicyDenied: {decision.reason}"}

        # 3. Deterministic Idempotency Key for safe checkpoint replay
        idem_raw = f"{ctx.tenant_id}:{ctx.task_id}:{ctx.step_index}:{tool_call_id}"
        idempotency_key = hashlib.sha256(idem_raw.encode()).hexdigest()

        # 4. Exchange user token for least-privilege scoped downstream OAuth token (never in prompt!)
        scoped_token = await self.secret_store.exchange_obo_token(ctx.user_oauth_token, scope=tool_name)

        # 5. Execute & emit structured audit log with correlation_id, actor, and model_version
        result = await self._invoke_downstream(tool_name, tool_input, scoped_token, idempotency_key)
        self.audit_logger.record(
            correlation_id=ctx.correlation_id,
            actor_id=decision.actor_id,
            tenant_id=ctx.tenant_id,
            model_version=ctx.model_version,
            tool_name=tool_name,
            idempotency_key=idempotency_key,
            status="SUCCESS"
        )
        return result
